title: Kafka Performance Handbook: Batching, Fetching, ISR & the Throughput-Latency Trade
summary: A dense study-notes series covering how Kafka producers batch and compress, how consumers tune fetches, how ISR and acks shape durability, and how every setting trades throughput against latency.

chapters.title: 1. Why Kafka Is Fast: The Mental Model
points: Kafka's speed comes from sequential disk I/O, an append-only log, and zero-copy transfer (sendfile) — not from avoiding disk
Log is partitioned; parallelism unit = partition count, so a 12-partition topic can serve 12 consumers in one group
Producer/consumer are the tunable ends; broker does almost no per-message work (no in-flight transformation)
Page cache: Kafka relies on OS page cache, not JVM heap, so warm cache ≫ bigger heap for broker tuning
Two competing goals: throughput (msgs/sec, MB/sec) vs latency (p99 end-to-end ms) — most configs move one at the expense of the other
The three knobs we'll tune: batching+compression (producer side), fetch behavior (consumer side), acks+ISR (durability side)
Benchmark honestly: measure with your payload size and partition count; defaults are tuned for durability, not speed
latency budget example: linger.ms 0 → p99 ~5ms but 80k msg/s; linger.ms 10 → p99 ~25ms but 400k msg/s on same hardware

chapters.title: 2. Producer Batching Mechanics
points: Producer groups records per partition into a ProducerBatch held in the RecordAccumulator; one batch = one network request per partition
batch.size (default 16KB): a batch is sent when full — bigger batches = fewer requests, better compression ratio
linger.ms (default 0): max time a half-full batch waits before being sent; this is the deliberate latency tax
Batch closes when EITHER batch.size OR linger.ms hits first — set both together, e.g. 64KB / 5-10ms
buffer.memory (default 32MB): total memory for unsent batches; producers block (or error, per max.block.ms) when full — a backpressure signal your consumers/producers are outpacing
Each partition has its own batch queue: many partitions dilute batching (a 64KB batch filled by 1 msg/partition wastes memory)
enable.idempotence=true changes defaults to acks=all, retries=Integer.MAX_VALUE — batching still applies on top
Rule of thumb: throughput workload → linger.ms 5-20ms; latency-sensitive → linger.ms 0-1ms and accept smaller batches
Watch batch-size-avg metric: if it's much smaller than batch.size, you're paying request overhead for nothing

chapters.title: 3. Compression: Which Codec and When
points: compression.type is set on the PRODUCER (gzip, snappy, lz4, zstd, none); batches are compressed whole, so batching directly improves compression ratio
Trade-off per codec: none (no CPU, big), lz4/snappy (fast, mild ratio), gzip (small, CPU-heavy), zstd (best ratio/speed balance, Kafka ≥2.1)
Compression saves network + broker disk; costs producer CPU — brokers store batches as-is unless broker-side recompression is configured
Broker compression.type=producer (default) means no recompression — keep it that way or you burn broker CPU twice
Measure end-to-end: producer CPU ↑, but consumer fetch CPU ↑ too (decompression) while network ↓ — benchmark with real payloads
JSON payloads compress 5-10x; already-compressed data (avro w/ compression, images) → don't recompress
compression works per-batch: linger.ms=0 + tiny batches = barely any compression benefit
Recommendation: default lz4; zstd when bandwidth/disk dominates and you can spare producer CPU

chapters.title: 4. Consumer Fetch Tuning
points: Consumers pull (long-poll fetch), they aren't pushed — fetch.min.bytes (default 1) = broker waits to accumulate data before responding
fetch.max.wait.ms (default 500ms): how long broker holds a fetch when min.bytes isn't met — this is the consumer-side latency cap
Throughput recipe: fetch.min.bytes=64KB+ with fetch.max.wait.ms=100-500 → fewer, bigger requests, higher latency for empty topics
max.partition.fetch.bytes (default 1MB): max per-partition data per fetch; must exceed largest single message or the consumer stalls forever
fetch.max.bytes (default 50MB): total cap per fetch — an upper bound, not a target
max.poll.records (default 500): records returned per poll() — bounds processing batch size and memory in your app
Latency recipe: fetch.min.bytes=1 (default) → responds as soon as any data exists; tune max.poll.interval.ms to exceed your worst processing time or you get a rebalance
Session/heartbeat: heartbeat.interval.ms and session.timeout.ms affect rebalance speed, not fetch throughput — don't confuse the two
Gotcha: a single oversized message larger than max.partition.fetch.bytes throws and blocks the partition forever — validate producer-side max size

chapters.title: 5. Replication, ISR and acks=all
points: Each partition has 1 leader + N follower replicas; followers fetch from the leader exactly like consumers
ISR (In-Sync Replicas) = followers fully caught up within replica.lag.time.max.ms (default 30s); lagging followers get kicked out
acks=0: fire-and-forget, no broker ack — max throughput, data lost on any failure
acks=1: leader acks after writing to its own log — lost if leader dies before followers replicate (the classic data-loss window)
acks=all (with min.insync.replicas≥2): ack only after all ISR replicas have the record — durable, highest latency
min.insync.replicas (broker/topic, default 1): minimum ISR required to accept writes; with acks=all and ISR shrunk below it, producers get NOT_ENOUGH_REPLICAS errors (a feature, not a bug)
Safe config: replication.factor=3, min.insync.replicas=2, acks=all → survives 1 broker failure with zero loss
unclean.leader.election.enable=false (default): never let a lagging replica become leader — availability dropped for consistency
Latency cost of acks=all ≈ one extra network hop + fsync on follower, typically single-digit ms, not 10x

chapters.title: 6. Durability on the Consumer Side
points: At-least-once: commit AFTER processing; crash → redelivery (need idempotent consumers), the safe default
At-most-once: commit BEFORE processing; crash → message dropped, only OK when loss is tolerable (metrics, telemetry)
Exactly-once = idempotent producer + transactions + read_committed consumers — mostly matters for consume-process-produce pipelines (Kafka Streams)
enable.auto.commit=true (default) commits every auto.commit.interval.ms (5s) on the next poll — can commit offsets for records never processed on crash → duplicates or loss
Manual commit: commitSync (blocks, reliable) vs commitAsync (non-blocking, may commit stale offsets — pair with a final commitSync on shutdown)
Commit per batch/partition, not per record: per-record commits serialize against the broker and crush throughput
Rebalance loses in-flight work: commit (or checkpoint) inside ConsumerRebalanceListener.onPartitionsRevoked
Duplicate handling is cheap: idempotent writes keyed by event ID or dedupe window — design for at-least-once + dedupe

chapters.title: 7. Throughput vs Latency: The Trade-off Map
points: Core pattern: everything that waits-and-amortizes (linger, fetch.min.bytes, big batches) buys throughput with latency; everything that sends immediately buys latency with overhead
Producer axis: linger.ms & batch.size ↑ = fewer requests/sec, better compression, higher p99
Consumer axis: fetch.min.bytes ↑ = broker-side batching, but cold topics feel it (capped by fetch.max.wait.ms)
Durability axis: acks 0→1→all trades latency+loss-risk for safety; compression trades CPU for network/disk
Latency is tail latency: one batch delay + one rebalance + one GC pause dominates p99 — measure p99/p999, never the average
Queueing math intuition: at ~70% utilization, queuing delays explode; headroom matters more than micro-tuning

Workload archetypes: telemetry/log shipping → maximize throughput (linger 10ms, lz4, acks=1 maybe, fetch.min.bytes 100KB); payments/orders → minimize latency+loss (linger 0-1ms, acks=all, min.isr=2, fetch.min.bytes=1)
You can't optimize both at once — pick per-topic configs: Kafka allows topic-level overrides for min.isr, cleanup policy, etc.

chapters.title: 8. Common Mistakes & Smells
points: Raising partition count to fix consumer lag when the real problem is max.poll.interval.ms exceeded → rebalance storm → more lag (vicious cycle)
buffer.memory exhausted / 'exhausted' logs: batching too big for buffer or downstream slow — back off linger.ms or add buffer, but really fix the sink
min.insync.replicas=1 + acks=all = false security: you're paying acks=all latency for acks=1 durability
Setting batch.size huge (1MB) with linger.ms=0: batches rarely fill, you just waste accumulator memory
Compression misconfiguration: broker compression.type ≠ producer → double compression work on every message
Committing every record with commitSync in the loop: 10x throughput loss for no durability gain vs per-batch commits
Ignoring producer retries + idempotence: retries without enable.idempotence can duplicate on retry — duplicates land in consumer dedupe budget
Tiny fetch.max.wait.ms (e.g. 10ms) + high fetch.min.bytes: broker busy-loops on polls, CPU burn on both ends
Benchmarking with default 1KB payloads: real JSON of 2-5KB changes batching, compression, and fetch math entirely

chapters.title: 9. Tuning Cheat Sheet & Summary
points: Producer defaults-to-fast template: linger.ms=5-10, batch.size=64KB, compression=lz4, buffer.memory=64MB, enable.idempotence=true, acks=all
Producer latency-first template: linger.ms=0-1, batch.size=16KB, compression=none or lz4, acks=all + min.isr=2
Consumer throughput template: fetch.min.bytes=65536, fetch.max.wait.ms=250, max.poll.records=1000, max.partition.fetch.bytes=4MB
Consumer latency-first template: fetch.min.bytes=1, max.poll.records=100-500, manual commitSync per batch
Broker durability template: replication.factor=3, min.insync.replicas=2, unclean.leader.election.enable=false, broker compression.type=producer
Metrics to watch: producer batch-size-avg & record-queue-time, request-latency-avg; consumer fetch-manager fetch-size-avg & poll idle time; broker under-replicated-partitions (>0 = act now)
Load-test order: fix consumer lag first (it backs up everything), then producer batching, then compression, then durability knobs last
One-sentence summary: batch to amortize, compress to shrink, fetch bigger to pull cheaper, ack on ISR to not lose — every knob just picks your spot on the throughput-latency curve
